personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Harry is defined by a layered personality that includes courage, loyalty, and a strong moral compass, but also adolescent volatility, stubbornness, pride, and a persistent inner conflict between wanting to belong and being set apart by fame. He is sardonic and dry when with Ron and Hermione ('Even inside his head the words sounded stupid'), genuinely frightened but outwardly stoic, and privately self-critical. His voice is informal, sometimes clipped, occasionally angry. He processes emotions internally at great length — his night of waking after the scar dream, his slow deliberations about who to write, his shame at worrying Ron might think him a coward. He tends toward understatement in direct speech and overstatement in internal thought. He resists being defined by his fame, is uncomfortable with being looked at, and bristles at condescension. He also displays a wry humor that sharpens under pressure ('I'll be at Ron's when you get back') and a capacity for spite that is humanizing rather than villainous (his satisfaction at manipulating Uncle Vernon, his petty internal dismissal of Cedric after Cho reveals she's going with him). He shows genuine bravery not as heroic performance but as reluctant necessity.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the most prominent surface traits: Harry is brave, loyal, morally upright, uncomfortable with attention ('No,' said flatly to Rita Skeeter's questions; 'I didn't enter' repeated with increasing irritation), and emotionally reactive. Daniel Radcliffe's performance conveys anxiety before tasks, warmth with friends, and directness in confrontation. Key lines translate recognizably: his reconciliation with Ron is terse and genuine ('Caught on, have you? Took you long enough' / 'It's okay. Forget it'), his defiance toward Voldemort is intact ('No' to bowing; 'I won't!' breaking the Imperius Curse), and his instinct to act without being asked (shouting the warning to Cedric in the maze, attempting to save Fleur's sister) is clearly shown. His voice pattern — short, declarative, frequently uncomfortable with emotional performance — is preserved.
personality_voice.difference: Several secondary and tertiary personality traits are reduced or absent in the film. The rich internal commentary that reveals Harry's sardonic self-awareness is eliminated by medium (no narration), but this affects characterization only where it surfaces in behavior. More significantly: (1) Harry's pride and stubbornness as a long-term trait is compressed — the book Harry refuses Ron's implicit forgiveness for two weeks and explicitly conditions the reconciliation on Ron admitting he was wrong; the film Harry capitulates quickly after the first task. (2) Harry's adolescent petty side (mentally dismissing Cedric as a 'useless pretty boy' after hearing about Cho, his internal gloating over Vernon) is absent from the film because it is entirely internal. (3) His complex relationship to fame — the way he is simultaneously irritated by it, helpless before it, and occasionally flattered by it — is reduced to simple discomfort. (4) His voice under extreme stress in the graveyard is largely intact, but the film does not show the private terror and determination ('He was not going to die crouching here like a child playing hide-and-seek') that makes his conduct there feel earned rather than generic.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The film preserves enough of Harry's core behavioral patterns — bravery, moral stubbornness, awkward loyalty, brief sarcasm, discomfort with attention — to remain clearly recognizable. The losses are mostly internal texture and secondary traits that do not individually constitute defining characterization, but in aggregate they simplify the character. The compression of his standoff with Ron (book: weeks of wounded pride; film: resolved in minutes) removes an important demonstration of his stubbornness and capacity for resentment. The absence of internal monologue eliminates his wry voice, his self-doubt, and his adolescent spite, which together constitute a significant portion of what makes the book Harry feel complete rather than symbolic. A minor deduction is warranted — not enough to drop into the 14-17 range because the primary traits are faithfully reproduced, but enough to prevent full marks.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Harry is the primary agent of virtually every scene he inhabits. He initiates (writing to Sirius after the dream, sneaking to the dragon enclosure, deciding to tell Cedric about the dragons, sending Hedwig, deciphering the egg in the prefects' bathroom), reacts (the graveyard confrontation), solves (the Summoning Charm solution arrived at through his own effort with Hermione's help), confronts (Mr. Crouch in the forest, Voldemort in the graveyard), and emotionally drives the story forward through his choices. Crucially, several of his book-specific acts of agency are plot-essential: he tells Cedric about the dragons unprompted and unambiguously on moral grounds; he figures out the gillyweed solution through sustained library research before Dobby brings it to him; he actively pieces together the Barty Crouch Jr./Moody connection through the Pensieve; he chooses to share the Triwizard winnings with Fred and George; he actively summons his Firebolt by first reasoning through what he's good at (with Moody's hints); and he navigates the maze using a range of newly learned spells.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Harry's central protagonist role throughout. He makes the key decisions of the tasks: he summons the Firebolt, he navigates the maze, he decides to share the cup with Cedric, he summons it back at the end. In the graveyard he resists the Cruciatus Curse and breaks the wand connection. He tells Dumbledore about the dream immediately and acts on it. He identifies the Pensieve and falls into it. He exposes Barty Crouch Jr. (or at minimum participates in the unmasking). His warning to Cedric about the dragons is present, his saving of Fleur's sister during the second task is present.
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several important acts of agency are transferred, compressed, or removed: (1) The gillyweed solution in the books is reached through weeks of sustained library effort by Harry and Hermione, then brought at the last minute by Dobby after Dobby overhears McGonagall and Moody discussing Harry's problem. In the film, Neville simply hands Harry the gillyweed with minimal dramatic preparation, and the role of Harry's active (if insufficient) research effort is eliminated. The solution arrives as a gift rather than through any agency on Harry's part. (2) The Summoning Charm solution (Accio Firebolt) in the books is reached through Harry working out the logic with Moody's oblique help and then executing sustained practice with Hermione. In the film the solution is similarly present but the extended preparation arc is compressed to near-invisibility. (3) Harry's decision to tell Cedric about the dragons in the books is a notable act of moral agency — he arranges it deliberately and takes a risk. In the film it is present but given no significant build-up. (4) The Pensieve investigation — Harry's active participation in understanding Barty Jr.'s history and the Crouch family dynamics — is compressed; much of what Harry learns and processes is transferred to Dumbledore's exposition. (5) Harry's decision to give the prize money to Fred and George (with his explicit reasoning about needing laughter) is absent from the theatrical film.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Harry retains protagonist status and his major decisions are preserved. However, the gillyweed resolution is a notable transfer of agency — in the books Harry actively contributes to the solution through sustained effort even if Dobby delivers it; in the film Neville simply provides it without any prior effort on Harry's part being visible. The Summoning Charm solution is intact as an act of agency in the task itself but its preparation arc is invisible, reducing the sense that Harry earned it. The loss of the prize money gift removes one of Harry's most generous and perceptive acts of the entire novel. These are meaningful reductions, though none individually rises to the level of a major function transfer. Collectively they reduce the texture of his agency without eliminating it.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Harry's motivations in GoF are layered: (1) survival and fear — he didn't ask to be in the tournament and is genuinely terrified; (2) pride and the desire not to appear weak or cowardly — a powerful secondary motivation that drives many choices, including refusing to look frightened in front of Ron, not begging Voldemort for mercy, competing on his own terms; (3) loyalty — to Cedric (warning him, sharing the cup, retrieving his body), to Ron and Hermione, to Sirius; (4) moral obligation — telling Cedric about the dragons when he could have kept the advantage; retrieving all four hostages rather than just Ron; (5) a deep need for parental figures and belonging — explicitly stated in his longing for 'someone like a parent' and his relationship with Sirius. His internal conflict centres on reconciling his desire to be ordinary ('just wanted to be') with his extraordinary circumstances, and between self-preservation and doing what he believes is right. He also struggles with jealousy toward Cedric (Cho), resentment toward Ron, guilt over entering the tournament even though he didn't enter it.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film captures Harry's fear and reluctance clearly — 'I don't want eternal glory. I just wanna be' is an explicit statement of his core motivation. His loyalty to Cedric drives the sharing of the cup and the body retrieval. His moral fiber is shown in the second task. His need for Sirius as a parental figure is briefly conveyed in their fireplace scene. His defiance of Voldemort in the graveyard is properly motivated by refusal to give him the satisfaction rather than any hope of winning.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: Several motivational threads are absent or underexplored: (1) Harry's complex relationship to his own fame as a source of both discomfort and occasional pride — present in the books through internal reflection, invisible in the film. (2) His jealousy of Cedric over Cho (a humanizing motivation that also adds texture to his behavior in the maze) is entirely absent from the theatrical film since the scene where he asks Cho and learns she's going with Cedric was cut. (3) His guilt and self-blame about Sirius returning to danger because of his letter — a motivating anxiety that drives several scenes in the book — is reduced to a single brief fireplace conversation. (4) His internal conflict about whether he wishes he could simply escape versus feeling bound by circumstances is present in the film ('I'm not ready for this') but not developed beyond that line. (5) The motivation underlying his decision to give Fred and George the prize money — explicitly to provide laughter and counter despair — is absent because the scene is absent.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: The core motivations are present and sufficiently coherent: Harry fears dying, wants to protect his friends, refuses to capitulate to Voldemort out of pride and moral commitment, and craves belonging. The film doesn't change these motivations — it simply under-explains them. 'Poorly explained but still correct' applies here more than 'changed.' The main penalty is for the complete loss of the jealousy/romantic motivation (Cho/Cedric thread was entirely cut in theatrical) and the compression of the Sirius-as-parental-figure motivation, which loses the specific emotional texture of Harry's longing for a parent figure. These represent simplification rather than replacement, warranting a score in the 11-13 range.

character_arc.book_baseline: Harry's arc in GoF moves from a relatively comfortable boy nearing the end of three years at Hogwarts — thrilled about the World Cup, excited about Hogwarts, feeling established in his world — through escalating terror and isolation (the tournament, Ron's betrayal, public hostility, the growing weight of Voldemort's return) to a climactic confrontation with death that forces him to mature rapidly. The arc has several specific stages: (1) the loss of security represented by the Dark Mark and Ron's betrayal; (2) the experience of being truly alone and unsupported in a dangerous competition; (3) the growing dread of Voldemort's return as scar-pain escalates; (4) the graveyard experience — witnessing Cedric's death, facing Voldemort, making the choice to die standing rather than crouching; (5) returning to a world where the truth is denied by authority and Harry must carry the knowledge of Voldemort's return essentially alone; (6) the final scene in the hospital wing where Mrs. Weasley holds him and he allows himself to break down — a moment of emotional integration. The arc's resolution is not triumph but traumatized maturity: Harry is older, his innocence is gone, his world has permanently changed. He chooses to give away the prize money — his last act — not out of generosity but because carrying it feels wrong.
character_arc.difference: The film's arc follows the same basic trajectory and preserves several key emotional beats: the isolation during the tournament, the reconciliation with Ron after the first task, the graveyard confrontation, the return with Cedric's body, the confrontation with Dumbledore about what happened. However, significant arc steps are abbreviated or missing: (1) The sustained period of isolation and hostility from the school — spanning weeks in the book — is compressed into what feels like days in the film. Harry's arc of learning to endure social ostracism while continuing to function is effectively absent. (2) The Sirius relationship as a sustained source of hope and anxiety across the year — with letters arriving progressively, the cave meeting, the growing understanding between them — is reduced to two brief scenes, removing the arc's emotional backbone outside of the tournament itself. (3) The preparation arc for each task (weeks of research and practice for the second task; the night before the third) is compressed, making Harry's progression feel less earned. (4) The ending arc — the hospital wing breakdown, the confrontation with Fudge, the decision to give away the money, the quiet talk with Dumbledore — is present but truncated. The film ends on a note of companionship (Harry, Ron, Hermione watching the ships leave) that is tonally different from the book's more subdued, trauma-aware conclusion. (5) The cutting of the Pensieve sequence to its essentials means Harry's gradual understanding of Barty Jr.'s history — an important stage in his developing comprehension of the wizarding world's moral complexity — is barely conveyed.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc exists in the film and reaches the correct destination: Harry survives, Cedric is dead, Voldemort has returned, Harry is traumatized but standing. But important steps are either rushed (the isolation arc, the preparation arc) or missing (the full emotional scope of the graveyard aftermath, the prize money renunciation, the sustained Sirius relationship). The film also softens the ending's tone, removing the specific note of traumatized maturity and replacing it with a more conventionally hopeful send-off. This represents incomplete arc preservation — the shape is there, but crucial stages are skipped or rushed. A score in the 8-10 range is appropriate: the arc is incomplete but recognizable.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Harry's key relationships in GoF are: (1) Ron — best friend, but here characterized by a significant rupture (Ron's jealousy and refusal to believe Harry) lasting weeks, resolved only after the first task proves Harry's sincerity; this rupture is important because it reveals both Ron's insecurity and Harry's capacity for genuine hurt and stubbornness. (2) Hermione — the intellectual backbone of the trio, Harry's moral anchor, whose relationship with him is uncomplicated but warm; she is his most reliable supporter throughout. (3) Sirius — Harry's most important adult relationship, functioning explicitly as a parental substitute; Harry's longing for him is one of the book's central emotional threads. (4) Hagrid — another parental figure, simpler than Sirius but deeply important; Harry's gratitude and loyalty to him is a recurring minor arc. (5) Dumbledore — a figure of authority Harry trusts but cannot fully access; their relationship deepens in the Pensieve scene and the post-graveyard conversation. (6) Cedric — a rival who becomes an ally; Harry's moral generosity toward him (warning about dragons, sharing the cup, bringing back his body) defines Harry's character more than almost anything else in the book.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: Ron's jealousy and the rupture are present in the film, though compressed: Ron refuses to speak to Harry for a brief period, reconciles after the first task. The emotional dynamic is broadly correct but lacks the sustained antagonism of the book. Hermione's role as supporter is preserved. Sirius appears twice (both times briefly) and the parental dynamic is gestured at but not developed. Hagrid's relationship with Harry is reduced to a few warm exchanges. Dumbledore's post-graveyard conversation with Harry is present and emotionally significant. The Cedric relationship — rival-to-ally — is adequately conveyed, culminating in the cup-sharing and body-retrieval.
key_relationships.difference: The Ron rupture loses its defining duration: in the book it is weeks of isolation that genuinely affects Harry's daily functioning; in the film it is resolved within what appears to be hours or days. This removes the demonstration of both characters' stubbornness. The Sirius relationship — arguably Harry's most emotionally important in the book — is drastically reduced: only two brief scenes survive, neither of which conveys the extended back-and-forth of letters, the cave meeting, or the depth of Harry's specific longing for a paternal figure. The line 'He needed someone like a parent' is one of the most important in the book for Harry's psychology and has no filmic equivalent. The Pensieve scene with Dumbledore is compressed, removing much of the trust and understanding built between them. The Hagrid relationship is present but thin.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: The most significant relationship loss is Sirius: the emotional dynamic that should define Harry's year is reduced to two brief, functional exchanges. The Ron rupture loses its weight due to compression. The Dumbledore relationship is present but the Pensieve's revelations — which deepen the relationship significantly — are compressed. Other relationships (Hermione, Cedric, Hagrid) are adequately preserved. The Sirius reduction alone constitutes a meaningful change in emotional dynamic, not just compression, because it removes the central adult relationship that makes Harry's vulnerability and longing visible throughout the year.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: GoF is the longest and most psychologically complex of the early Potter novels, and much of its texture comes from material that is not directly plot-essential: Harry's weeks-long social ostracism and how he functions within it; his private petty jealousy of Cedric; his sardonic internal commentary on Trelawney, Rita Skeeter, and the Dursleys; his complex relationship to his own fame; his night of insomnia after the dream; his embarrassment about the ball and the sustained comedy of getting a date; his growing understanding of the wizarding world's moral failures (Crouch's methods, the treatment of house-elves, the MInistry's denial); his relationship to Cedric as a genuinely complex figure rather than a simple martyr; the texture of his Hogwarts life (Divination classes, Potions with Snape, Care of Magical Creatures with the skrewts); his Pensieve experience and what it reveals about Barty Jr., Karkaroff, Bagman, and Snape; and his final renunciation of the prize money as an act of deliberate counter-programming against the tournament's logic of glory.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film retains the emotional core and the major plot beats. Harry's social isolation is briefly shown. His relationship with Ron is present. His graveyard experience is rendered with reasonable fidelity to the book's emotional register. The Pensieve visit is included (truncated). His moral choices in the tasks are present. The Cedric relationship is preserved at its most important moments.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The losses are substantial in aggregate. The entire domestic texture of Harry's life at Hogwarts — Trelawney's classes, the Divination homework comedy with Ron, the weeks of skrewt lessons, the sustained portrait of his ordinary school existence — is largely absent. His internal satirical voice, which provides much of the book's humor and humanizes him, is entirely unavailable in film form and nothing replaces it. The Sirius relationship loses its full emotional weight. The Barty Crouch Jr. backstory and its moral implications — which Harry processes through the Pensieve into an understanding of the wizarding world's capacity for injustice — is reduced to a brief narrative delivery. The house-elf subplot (Harry's dawning awareness of injustice, which doesn't fully take hold for him but begins here) is entirely absent from the film. The Rita Skeeter subplot resolution (Hermione catching her as a beetle, the full revenge narrative) is present in truncated form. Harry's prize money decision is absent. The Neville backstory revelation — which Harry must sit with, unable to share, because Dumbledore asks him to keep the secret — and what it reveals about Harry's capacity for empathy and discretion, is absent from the film. The sustained portrait of Harry as a person navigating a school year — with homework, classes, rivalries, embarrassments, and small joys — is compressed almost to nothing.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The film removes a significant portion of the material that makes GoF's Harry more than a protagonist in an adventure: his internal life, his comic sensibility, his domestic ordinariness, his moral processing of complex injustices, his relationships with secondary characters, and his private emotional responses. What survives is primarily the plot skeleton and the most visible emotional beats. This constitutes 'noticeable simplification; important nuances, relationships, agency, or contradictions are missing' — the 8-10 range. The film does not flatten Harry into a single trait, and enough of his complexity survives that he is not merely functional. But a reader of the book who watches the film would find substantial portions of what they valued most about Harry in this installment to be absent.

Harry's sustained social ostracism across multiple weeks of the school year — compressed to brief days in film
Harry's private petty jealousy of Cedric regarding Cho Chang — absent (theatrical cut removed the asking-Cho scene entirely)
Harry's refusal to reconcile with Ron until Ron explicitly apologizes — compressed; film Harry forgives almost immediately
Harry's sustained library research for the second task (weeks of effort before Dobby's intervention) — replaced by Neville simply handing over gillyweed
Harry's moral processing of the Pensieve revelations (Barty Jr.'s history, Bagman's trial, Snape's past, Karkaroff's evidence) — heavily truncated in film
Harry's decision to give the Triwizard prize money to Fred and George, with explicit reasoning — absent from theatrical film
Harry's sustained relationship with Sirius across the year (multiple letters, cave meeting, growing trust) — reduced to two brief scenes
Harry's private understanding that he longs for 'someone like a parent' — absent from film
Harry's keeping of Neville's parents' secret as an act of empathy and discretion — absent from film (Neville backstory is absent)
Harry's sardonic internal commentary on Trelawney, Skeeter, Dursleys — unavailable in film form, not replaced by observable behavior
Harry's complex relationship to his own fame — compressed to simple discomfort

Harry's experience of Voldemort's Cruciatus Curse as a character-defining test of will ('I WON'T!' breaking the Imperius Curse earlier) — Imperius scene present, Cruciatus resistance compressed in graveyard
Harry's deliberate manipulation of Uncle Vernon using the Sirius threat — absent from film (Dursley opening missing from theatrical release)
The house-elf subplot and Harry's nascent awareness of systemic injustice — entirely absent from the film
The full Rita Skeeter subplot resolution (Hermione's beetle discovery, its implications) — truncated

key_observations: The film's Harry Potter is a faithful rendering of the character's most visible and plot-essential traits — his bravery under duress, moral stubbornness, awkward loyalty, discomfort with fame, and refusal to capitulate before Voldemort. The major emotional beats of the novel are reproduced with reasonable fidelity, and Daniel Radcliffe's performance conveys the core personality. The primary losses are architectural rather than surface-level: the sustained inner life that constitutes much of the book's characterization (sardonic humor, private jealousy, adolescent pettiness, chronic self-doubt, the specific longing for parental connection) is unavailable in film form and not compensated for by behavioral equivalents. The Sirius relationship — the emotional center of Harry's year — is drastically reduced. Several acts of agency are compressed or transferred. The arc reaches its correct destination but skips important preparatory stages. The result is a Harry who is recognizable as himself but substantially simpler than his book counterpart: an adventure protagonist rather than a fully rendered adolescent. A score of 73 reflects this — clearly faithful in its broad strokes, meaningfully incomplete in its texture.
